did_you_know.text: The name Edom is related to the word “red,” recalling Esau’s connection with the color red earlier in the story of his birthright.
The names of Esau’s wives differ slightly in other lists in Genesis. Scholars see this as an example of ancient texts preserving variant forms of names.
The reason Esau and Jacob separated resembles the earlier separation of Abraham and Lot: the land could not support both large herds together.
Mount Seir was a mountainous region south and east of the Dead Sea, and it became associated with Edom.
The name Teman later became associated with a region or group in Edom, so it also appears in prophecies about Edom.
Amalek is presented here as a descendant of Esau. Later in the Bible, Amalek becomes a major enemy of Israel, but this chapter itself is a genealogy, not a war story.
The word “chief” is a title for a family or tribal leader, not merely a personal name. Some translations render it as “chieftain,” “leader,” or “duke.”
The name Korah appears here in two different branches of Esau’s family: among Eliphaz’s descendants and among Oholibamah’s sons. The same name does not prove that the person is the same.
The Horites, the descendants of Seir, are presented as inhabitants of the land before Esau’s family is listed. The chapter thus preserves a memory of an earlier population in the region of Edom.
The word “yemim” is rare, and its meaning is uncertain. Translations and commentators have suggested different possibilities, including hot springs or creatures associated with mules.
This verse distinguishes Edom’s kings from the time before Israel had a king. Its wording presents Edom’s history from a viewpoint familiar with Israelite kingship.
The chapter lists eight kings of Edom, and many come from different cities or regions rather than being described as father and son. This differs from a list of one royal dynasty.
Compared with most people in the list, the text gives unusually detailed information about the maternal ancestry of the king’s wife, Mehetabel.
The chapter contains two lists of Edomite chiefs, but their names are not identical. They may reflect different groups, places, or periods in the organization of Edom.
